Existence and implementation of national diabetes prevention and
control plan

To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for diabetes prevention
and control at national level.

Country has a national diabetes prevention and control plan developed/
updated within the past 5 years and the plan is currently implemented.
● A national diabetes prevention and control plan includes a set of specific
strategic actions to be taken to achieve the goals of the national diabetes
prevention and control programme. The plan may be an independent
diabetes prevention and control plan or part of a comprehensive national
plan for noncommunicable diseases.

Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have a national
plan that includes prevention, early detection, treatment and/or care for
diabetes?” and needs to provide a copy of the plan and the latest report on the
implementation of the plan.
Existence of the plan is validated by examining the plan document and
implementation is validated by examining the latest report detailing the
execution of at least one strategic action outlined in the plan.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has a national diabetes
prevention and control plan developed/updated within the past 5 years and the
plan is currently being implemented.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has a national diabetes
prevention and control plan developed/updated within the past 5 years, but it is
not currently being implemented.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country does not have a national diabetes
prevention and control plan developed/updated within the past 5 years.
Type of diabetes included in the plan
NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report

An acceptable minimum number of strategic actions completed according to
plan must be defined at every evaluation period to consider the plan as currently
implemented.

WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
NCD country capacity survey [website]. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2023 (https://www.who.int/teams/ncds/surveillance/monitoring-capacity/

Existence and implementation of policies and/or legislation for
diabetes prevention
To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for diabetes prevention.

Country has adopted policies and/or legislation aimed at preventing diabetes
and its risk factors, and the policies and/or legislation are currently being
implemented.
National diabetes prevention policies include the country’s vision, priorities,
budgetary decisions and course of action for diabetes prevention. A policy or
legislation may be an independent diabetes prevention policy/legislation or part
of a comprehensive noncommunicable diseases policy/legislation.
This indicator excludes assessment of tax laws.

Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Has the country adopted national
policies and/or legislation aimed at preventing diabetes and its risk factors?” and
needs to provide a copy of the policies and legislations and the latest report on
their implementation.
Existence of policies and/or legislation is validated by examining policy/
legislation documents and implementation is validated by examining the latest
report detailing the execution of policies and legislations.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has adopted policies and/or
legislation aimed at preventing diabetes and its risk factors, that are currently
being implemented.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has adopted policies
and/or legislation aimed at preventing diabetes and its risk factors, but these are
not currently being implemented.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has not adopted policies and/or
legislation.
NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report

An acceptable minimum number of policies and/or legislation implemented
according to plan must be defined every evaluation period to consider the
policies and/or legislation as currently implemented.

WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
NCD country capacity survey [website]. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2023 (https://www.who.int/teams/ncds/surveillance/monitoring-capacity/
ncdccs, accessed 26 May 2024).

Existence and enforcement of health taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco,
sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed food, foods high in saturated
fats, trans fats, free sugars and/or salt

To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for reducing risk factors for
diabetes and diabetes-related complications.

Country has adopted health taxes on one or more of the following items:
alcoholic beverages, tobacco, sugar-sweetened beverages, foods high in
saturated fats, trans fats, foods high in free sugars, foods high in salt, and these
health taxes are being enforced.
● Health taxes are excise taxes levied on products that have a negative
public health impact, for example, tobacco, alcohol and other non-
alcoholic beverages and food products high in sugar, saturated fats, trans
fats and/or salt.

Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Has the country adopted health
taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-
processed foods, foods high in saturated fats, trans fats, free sugars and/or salt?”,
and needs to provide a copy of the tax policy/legislation and the latest report on
enforcement of health taxes.
Existence of health taxes is validated by examining tax legislation documents
and implementation is validated by examining the latest report(s) detailing the
enforcement of health taxes.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has adopted health taxes
on at least one type of forementioned products and the health taxes are
being enforced.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has adopted health taxes
on at least one type of forementioned products, but the health taxes are not
being enforced.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has not adopted health taxes on
at least one type of forementioned products.
Type of product, administrative level (district, provincial, or national)

Existence of national guidelines for diabetes management
To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for diabetes management.

The country has evidence-based national guidelines, protocols, standards, or
technical guidance for diabetes management in primary health care settings,
developed/updated within the past 5 years.
● National guidelines, protocols, standards or technical guidance are
information products endorsed by the ministry of health containing
recommendations for clinical management/practice.

Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have evidence-
based national guidelines, protocols, standards, or technical guidance for
diabetes management in primary health care settings?” and needs to provide
a copy of the national guidelines and the latest report on enforcement of
health taxes.
Existence of evidence-based national guidelines, protocols, standards or
technical guidance is validated by examining documents that outline the
scientific steps that were taken to develop the national guidelines, protocol,
standards or technical guidance.

Type of diabetes, type of services (e.g. diagnosis, treatment, diabetic foot
management, retinopathy management), type of diabetes complications

To assess the availability of referral and back-referral systems for clinical services
for advanced diabetes.

The country has a clearly defined and well-established functional referral
and back-referral system for diabetes management, facilitating the seamless
transition between primary care, secondary and tertiary care.

Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have a clearly
defined and well-established referral system between primary care, secondary
and tertiary care for diabetes management?” and needs to provide a copy of
relevant documents about the referral system.
Existence of a clearly defined, well-established functional referral system is
validated by examining documents that outline mechanisms for referral from
primary care to secondary and tertiary care, as well as feedback mechanisms
from higher to lower levels of care.

Inclusion of insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring in national health benefit package

To assess integration of insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring into national health benefit packages.

Country has a national health benefit package that includes insulin, insulin
delivery devices and blood glucose self-monitoring.
Health benefit packages define the high priority services in a country that should
be made available to all citizens from public funds.

Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have a national
health benefit package that includes insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood
glucose self-monitoring?” and needs to provide a copy of the national health
benefit package.
Inclusion of insulin and insulin delivery devices in the national health benefit
package is validated by examining the national health benefit package document
for insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-monitoring coverage.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has a national health benefit
package that includes insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose
self-monitoring.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has a national health
benefit package that includes either insulin or insulin delivery devices or blood
glucose self-monitoring but not all.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has a national health benefit
package, but it does not include insulin, insulin delivery devices or blood glucose
self-monitoring.

Component of the indicator (insulin or insulin delivery devices or blood glucose
self-monitoring), type of diabetes, type of insulin, level of reimbursement (fully
reimbursed or partially reimbursed), age group of people who are included in the
benefit package, administrative level (national provincial/state/region or district).

Insulin, its delivery devices, and blood glucose self-monitoring affordability

To assess the affordability of insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose
self-monitoring.

Country has affordable insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring for people with diabetes. Affordability means that the monthly
expenses for people living with diabetes or their families, including expenditures
on basic needs represented by national poverty line (NPL), do not exceed the
minimum wage for the lowest paid government sector worker (LPGW).

The indicator is considered “Yes”, that is, affordable, if:
[(NPL +monthly cost for insulin, insulin devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring to person with diabetes) /LPGW wage] ≤1

Type of diabetes, type of insulin, type of insulin delivery device, type of blood
glucose self-monitoring.
Country report, survey, national health insurance claims database

A population-weighted average can be used to address differences in prices,
wages and size of population at sub-national levels.
When estimated expenses and wages are derived from different years, general
inflation rate and health care inflation rate must be included in the calculation.

Availability of trained health care staff for diabetes management
To assess the availability of high-quality services for diabetes management.

Proportion of health facilities in which staff have been trained in the latest WHO
or national guidelines on diabetes clinical management.

Number of health facilities in which staff have been trained in the latest
WHO or national guidelines on diabetes clinical management during the
reporting period.
“Staff” refers to physicians or other nationally authorized health professionals for
diabetes management. A multidisciplinary care team for diabetes management
may include the following:
● cardiologist
● diabetes nurse
● endocrinologist
● general practitioner
● homecare nurse
● nephrologist
● nutritionist
● ophthalmologist
● physiotherapist
● podiatrist

Facility level of care type, provider ownership type (public/private), facility
location type (urban/rural), training topic, type of health professional
Health facility report, health workforce information system or survey

Frequency of training depends on the date of the last version of WHO or national
guidelines, as well as the staff turnover at the health care facility.

Availability of diabetes, cardiovascular disease and hypertension
core medicines
To monitor supply of essential medicines for diabetes management.

Proportion of health facilities that have diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and
hypertension core medicines based on WHO or national treatment guidelines.
Diabetes core medicines include:
● metformin
● sulfonylurea
● insulin
Cardiovascular disease core medicines include:
● aspirin
● beta blockers
● statins
Hypertension core medicines include the following classes of medications:
● angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
● angiotensin-receptor blockers
● long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
● thiazide and thiazide-like agents
Other core medicines may be added to the list as WHO and national guidelines
are updated.

Number of health facilities reporting “no stock-out” of diabetes, cardiovascular
disease and hypertension core medicines during the reporting period.

Type of medicine, type of insulin (short-acting human, intermediate acting
human, long-acting analogue), facility level of care type, provider ownership
type (public/private), facility location type (urban/rural).

Health facility medicine stock register, health facility report, logistics information

In some settings, health facilities do not dispense medicines so the reporting
units may be community medicine dispensaries/pharmacies.

Availability and quality of a diabetes surveillance system

To assess the availability of quality and comprehensive surveillance data for
diabetes programme management.

Country has an established diabetes surveillance system comprising of all
essential components if:
● Country conducts a standardized population-based health survey that
includes availability and quality of diabetes services every 3 to 5 years.
● Country has an electronic, standardized system for recording person- and
facility-level data that includes diabetes, with high level of coverage.
● Country has a type 1 diabetes registry with national level coverage.
● Country conducts regular standardized health facility surveys on
availability of health facility services including diabetes management
services and on capacities of health facilities to provide these services at
required standards of quality, every 1 to 3 years.
● Country has a well-functioning CRVS system for generating reliable
cause-specific mortality data on a routine basis. The International Form
of Medical Certificate of the Cause of Death is completed by certifiers.
The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is used to code the
causes of death. Cause-of-death data are accessible to policy-makers and
researchers.

1. Country can respond “Yes” to the following questions:
● “Does your country conduct a population-based survey that includes
diabetes?”. The country indicates frequency of conducting the population-
based survey (the country is considered to have available a regular
standardized population-based survey that includes diabetes if there are
published survey statistics at least every 3 to 5 years).
● “Does your country have an electronic standardized system for
recording person-and facility-level data that includes diabetes in public
facilities?”(The country is considered to have an electronic standardized
system if it has an electronic type of system that covers more than 50% of
facilities).
● “Does your country have a type 1 diabetes registry?”, indicate
coverage (national, sub-national or others) and type (population- or
hospital-based).
● “Does your country conduct standardized surveys of facilities to assess
availability of health facility services including diabetes management
services and on capacities of health facilities to provide these services
at required standards of quality?” – indicate the year of last facility
survey (The country has available regular standardized health facility
surveys, if there are published survey statistics on availability, readiness,
quality, management, and financing of diabetes management services,
every 1 to 3 years).
Country needs to provide a copy of documents to support their response to
abovementioned questions.

2. Availability and quality of national civil registration and vital statistic systems
are assessed through submissions to the WHO mortality database. WHO
collects mortality data, including cause of death, from civil registration
systems in the WHO mortality database through a routine annual call for
data. Data quality is assessed through usability defined as percentage of all
deaths which are registered with meaningful cause-of-death information. The
system is considered to generate reliable cause-specific mortality data on a
routine basis if:
● Data from the five most recent reporting years are, on average, at least
70% usable. Usability is calculated as:
[(Completeness (%))*(1- Deaths assigned to a garbage code (%)].
● At least 5 years of cause-of-death data have been reported to WHO in the
last 10 years.
● The most recent year of data reported to WHO is no more than 5 years old.
The availability and quality of a diabetes surveillance system is validated
by examining documents that describe or evidence the existence of the
abovementioned essential components of a diabetes surveillance system.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has all the essential components
of a diabetes surveillance system.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has one or more, but not
all the essential components of a diabetes surveillance system.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has none of the essential
components of a diabetes surveillance system.

Chronic kidney disease assessment among people with diabetes

To assess the level of chronic kidney disease assessment among people with
diabetes in health facilities.

The proportion of people with diabetes registered in health facilities who were
assessed for diabetic kidney disease based on the following criteria:
● Presence of an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of <60mL/min
per 1.73m2 on at least two occasions, 1 to 3 months apart; and/or
● Presence of albuminuria in at least two urine samples, 1 to 3
months apart.
Urinary albumin excretion can be estimated in a spot urine sample using several
tests (from most preferred to least preferred):
● urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
● urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR)
● reagent strip (“dipstick”) urine analysis for albumin or total protein with
automated reading
● reagent strip (“dipstick”) urine analysis for albumin or total protein with
manual reading.
